content.thinking:
I need to plan the dimensions and whimsical style for this biplane in one pass since I'll be writing the whole file without feedback—thinking a Stearman/Jenny-like shape with roughly 7.5m wingspan, chubby fuselage, oversized cowl, big propeller, and a cheerful color palette.

I'm sketching out the joint skeleton: a root body joint, hinges for the propeller, wing ailerons, rudder, elevators, wheels, tailwheel steering, and possibly a pilot head joint for a scarf detail. I'm working out the coordinate placement for fuselage, wheels, and tail, being careful with joint API parameters like parent, position, direction, and hinge roles so everything stays structurally sound without being able to test-run it.

Now I'm defining the wheel joints with spin axes along their axles, then setting up the fuselage as a lofted shape running from tail to nose through catmull-interpolated stations with a circular cross-section.

For paint, I'm going with cheerful, storybook colors rather than heavy toon-shader effects—plain colors combined with gradients, patches, and wood grain, plus SVG decals for lettering, numbers, roundels, and stripes applied onto the curved fuselage surface.

Working out decal placement on the curved fuselage is tricky since I need a surface hit point rather than guessing coordinates, so I'm considering using a surface query to find the right position before applying the decal, to avoid projection errors on the curved geometry.

I'll use text sparingly for a decal number like "No. 7," since fonts should render fine in-browser even if the specific style falls back. Now I'm working out the plane's actual dimensions in meters — fuselage running from the nose cowl around z≈2.1 back to the tail near z≈-3.0, with the centerline height tapering slightly from the engine to the tail.

I'm calculating overall proportions: landing gear axle height, strut lengths, fuselage radius narrowing toward the cockpit, and making sure the propeller and top wing clear the ground with some whimsical oversized scale. Total height lands around 2.9 meters, wingspan roughly 7.4 at top and 6.6 at bottom, chord 1.25 meters, length about 6 meters nose to tail — now I'm moving into extruding the wing shapes with an airfoil profile.

Thinking through how to orient the extrusion axes so the plan-view outline maps correctly to the model's coordinate system, then weighing whether a flat beveled slab is good enough versus lofting a true airfoil cross-section swept along the span with rounded wingtip caps for a more whimsical, chunky look.

Rounded caps give a dome that extends about 0.62 beyond the path ends, adding a squashed whimsical bulge to the wingtip—total span comes to roughly 7.4 with chord half-width 0.62 along z.

I'm adding decorative paint to the wing: rib stripes running along the chord, countershaded lighter undersides, and a distinct tip color where the span exceeds a threshold, all driven by a paint function keyed on position and normal.

Figuring out texel density for the paint sheet given total wing and fuselage surface area, I settle on a 2048 paintSize for sharp rib lines around 2.5 cm wide, staying well under the 4096 atlas limit. I'm also planning interplane struts as paired elements on each side near the wingtips plus cabane struts near the fuselage.

Now I'm working out the flying wires as thin diagonal rods with small radius and cheap low-poly rings, figuring roughly two cross wires per bay across two bays. For wing placement, I'm positioning the top wing higher and slightly forward with stagger, and the bottom wing lower near the fuselage's bottom radius so it intersects slightly where it attaches, checking that the gap between wings relative to chord length gives a plausible ratio. I'm also sizing cabane struts to span from the fuselage top up to the top wing's position.

For the cockpit, I'm thinking through how to fake an open-cockpit look without true cutouts: using a dark flattened sphere inset into the fuselage top plus a torus for the leather coaming ring, with a pilot figure (jacketed torso sphere, helmeted head, goggles) poking up above the fuselage line. I'm placing the coaming ring near the fuselage top and considering a dark flattened cylinder as a simpler stand-in for the cockpit opening.

Now I'm sketching out the fuselage profile as a series of loft stations from tail to nose, each with a z-position, height, width, and thickness, tapering from a thin tail tip through a wider mid-section near the cockpit, peaking in width at the engine bay, then narrowing again before the engine cowl. I'm planning the cowl as a separate lathed, bulging round shape at the nose with an open front dark ring, possibly suggesting radial engine cylinders and a spinner for a whimsical touch.

Working out the cowl's hollow shell cross-section...

For the engine detail, I'm adding a dark recessed plate with a ring of small cylinders representing the radial engine, plus planning the propeller spinner cone at the front of the cowl.

Still writing propeller geometry...

Setting the propeller hub at z=2.0 with small bolt details on the hub plate, then moving to the tail assembly — planning the vertical fin as an extruded outline in the Y-Z plane with forward direction along Z.

I'm sketching the fin's outline coordinates near the fuselage top, with the leading edge further back and a slight taper, and separating out the rudder as its own hinged piece at the trailing edge.

Still defining fin outline...

Setting up the rudder bone with a hinge joint rotating about its vertical axis, then moving on to define the horizontal stabilizer and elevator outlines.

Still working out stabilizer geometry...

I'm checking that the stabilizer and elevator spans along z line up correctly with the hinge position, and verifying the rudder's hinge point doesn't spatially overlap with the elevator region since the rudder sits higher on the y-axis.

I'm adjusting the vertical tail positions to avoid overlap: lowering the stabilizer to y=1.5, raising the rudder base to y=1.6, and checking that the fuselage width at that z-position still contains the stabilizer root with a small clearance gap between the elevator and rudder base.

I'm also planning small support struts connecting the fuselage to the stabilizer underside, and working out how to model the ailerons as thin flap plates attached along the wing's trailing edge, spanning the outer wing sections with a shallow chord depth.

Defining aileron hinge geometry...

Working out the aileron and flap placement on the top wing's tapering tip, then setting similar proportions for the bottom wing which has a shorter chord and span.

I'm deciding on wing cross-section thickness and planning the paint scheme: cream top surfaces with tan rib striping, red wingtips past a certain span, and a lighter underside color.

Writing paint logic...

Writing decal placement logic...

Positioning the front and rear struts at staggered heights for top and bottom wings, using wood-toned coloring with grain detail for a varnished look.

Working out the cabane strut geometry, placing front and rear A-frame struts from the fuselage top to the top wing center at various x,y,z offsets, checking they embed properly at the fuselage surface and wing attachment points.

Now I'm figuring out the flying wires connecting strut feet to wing roots and cabane points diagonally, setting a small radius (around 0.01-0.012) for thin rod geometry and choosing a dark or silver color for the wire material.

Then I move on to the landing gear, sketching out the V-struts running from the lower fuselage down to the wheel axle, plus a rear strut forming a secondary support leg.

Working out the torus orientation for the tires and planning a black tire with cream hubcap discs, maybe adding simple spokes for a whimsical look.

Now I'm turning to the tail wheel assembly, figuring out its spring strut position from the fuselage underside down to a smaller torus wheel, making sure the main gear height places the fuselage bottom just touching the floor.

I'm also sketching out the exhaust pipes as curved Catmull-Rom sweeps running from the cowl sides down and back along the fuselage, plus deciding on separate hinge joints for the left and right wheels.

For surface details I'm planning a rivet-stud helper that merges small sphere geometries into rings for the cowl rim, and figuring out a decal-based swooping stripe pattern for the fuselage sides.

Now I'm settling on a cheerful barnstormer color palette: tomato red, cream, sunny yellow, teal, leather brown, plum, steel, and wood tones, deciding the fuselage should be the bold red-orange with cream accents and teal pops for contrast.

I'm defining the paint function for the hull with a cream belly, red sides, and a yellow stripe band wrapping along the fuselage's y-position to create a swoosh effect.

For the cowl rim I'm deciding yellow for the front lip and teal elsewhere, and thinking about adding a subtle countershading tone so top and bottom surfaces read with slightly different lightness for a storybook feel.

That countershading approach works nicely nested into the fuselage paint, lightening the top and darkening the belly for a hand-painted gradient look applied across the hull. Now I'm moving to the cockpit, sketching out a torus for the coaming ring.

Sizing the coaming radius against fuselage width, then adding the dark cockpit opening, pilot torso and head with helmet and goggles, and a flowing scarf ribbon sweeping back behind the neck for motion.

I'm checking the pilot head's position relative to the top wing to make sure it's visible past the trailing edge, then planning joints for the pilot — head bone for helmet/goggles, plus arms reaching forward to the control stick.

Now I'm adding a windscreen: a slanted trapezoid panel in teal-blue, positioned ahead of the cockpit, using a flat-colored frame since transparency isn't supported.

So a -25° tilt leans the windscreen backward correctly, and it sits right on top of the fuselage near the top wing without clipping. I'm adding a streamlined headrest fairing behind the cockpit as a tapering red capsule shape, then moving on to add a pitot tube and wingtip lights.

For the wingtip lights I'll use small glowing spheres, red on the left and green on the right to match real aircraft convention, and skip the landing lamp and strut lantern as unnecessary extras. I'm also considering adding a whimsical pennant string of triangular flags for a barnstormer feel, but routing it directly between the wingtip and tail would cross through other geometry, so I need a cleaner path for it.

Actually maybe a streamer from the wing tip to the tail fin top would pass behind the trailing edge at mid-length, checking the geometry to make sure it clears the wing rather than intersecting it.

Now I'm adding decorative hanging pennants - small triangular cards in red, yellow, teal, and cream colors, draped along a curved path and attached near the body for a whimsical touch, mirrored on both sides, with the path sagging slightly in the middle before ending near the top of the tail fin.

I'm figuring out the pennant orientation when seen from downstream — the wide root edge needs to sit at the bottom of the SVG with the apex pointing up, so I'm working out the triangle path coordinates accordingly.

For card facing, I'm reconsidering the flow axis: with flow along z, cards span along x and are only visible edge-on from the sides, so I think flipping flow to the x-axis would make the cards span along z instead, giving better visibility from the front/back and sides simultaneously.

For decorative details, I'm planning simple decals avoiding any copyrighted logos — maybe a painted name on the fuselage and a whimsical sun face emblem with rays and cheeks on the cowl sides for charm.

For the center point, I'll set it to the bounding-box middle of the fuselage sweep and cast the ray at azimuth 90, elevation 0 to find where it hits the side surface. Then I'll attach the decal to that hit point, bumping segments up to 16 so the tapered text reads cleanly on the curved side.

Thinking through orientation: a viewer standing at +X looking toward -X has their right pointing toward -Z, meaning text drawn on that side naturally reads nose-to-tail left-to-right, matching the real-world convention for aircraft lettering. On the opposite side, the viewer at -X looking toward +X has their right pointing toward +Z (the nose), so text there would read tail-to-nose if I just mirror it the same way—I need to check whether that matches how real planes handle the right-side lettering or if it needs to be flipped.

I'm settling on no mirroring: since the decal always faces the viewer directly, text drawn normally will appear correctly oriented on both the left and right sides without needing a mirror flag. I also want name decals on both sides plus a "7" on the tail fin, placed by raycasting onto the fin surface along the ±X direction. For the text rendering I'm using an SVG with Georgia serif bold font, which should render fine in headless Chrome, and I want to keep the total texture count modest since each one eats into atlas space.

For the pennants, rather than creating four separate small textures, I'm considering generating three colored pennant textures and passing them as a list to a single cards call so the renderer picks randomly among them, saving atlas budget. I'm planning a 4096 atlas sheet to comfortably fit everything.

For the cockpit, I'm adding small interior details like a seat, control stick with a red knob, and an instrument panel, even though they won't be very visible. I considered adding a decorative gravity fuel tank capsule on top of the center wing section but decided to skip it to keep the overall height around 2.7 rather than letting it creep up to 2.8.

I'm toying with whimsical extras like a wing-walker figure, but that adds too much height and complexity. Instead I'm leaning toward keeping a human pilot with big goofy goggles, and adding a second front cockpit with a cute teddy bear passenger — a brown sphere head with ears, a cream muzzle, nose, eyes, and a little scarf, positioned just under the wing with its own coaming ring, as a fun but moderate addition.

I'm now working out the fuselage geometry: placing two windscreens front and rear, figuring the coaming heights and radii at each station based on fuselage width, and sizing the pilot's torso capsule to fit through the cockpit opening. I'm also starting a details list for rivets and other small fuselage features.

For the rivet rows, I'm thinking through using raycasts against the fuselage surface to position small sphere studs along seam lines, roughly 16 per side spaced along z, keeping the total part count well under limits.

For panel lines, I'll keep it cheap by darkening thin bands directly in the hull paint texture at a few z positions (around 1.05, cockpit area, and -1.15) rather than modeling separate geometry.

Then I want to add rivet details around the engine cowl lip and a visible radial engine look: a dark plate near z=1.95 with a ring of small steel cylinders poking outward to suggest cylinder heads.

Now I'm placing those cylinder parts manually around the ring, then adding a center hub disc and a spinner dome shaped with a lathe profile, painting it with yellow and a red tip band near the top. I'm also thinking about giving the wheel hubcaps a sunburst decal using a texture on the plane geometry.

For the hubcap texture, I'm sketching a cream circle with alternating red and yellow rays, keeping it symmetric so the same texture works on both wheels. Then for the tire itself, I'm filling the torus's inner hole with a dark cylinder disc to look like a hub.

Now I'm sizing the torus and disc so the tire protrudes beyond the hub while keeping the decal recessed but visible, and considering a low-polygon torus with flat shading for a crisp faceted toy look.

I'm skipping fenders and finalizing the joint hierarchy — body root, propeller hinge, wheels, tail wheel, rudder, elevators, four ailerons, pilot/bear heads, and a control stick, all defined with `joint(name, {parent, at, dir, role})` using hinge or head roles.

Hinge axes need to align with each part's rotation axis: ailerons and elevators hinge along the span direction, rudder hinges vertically. For the fuselage, I'm setting up a loft along station points with elliptical cross-sections (width/2 and height/2 radii) bound to the body bone, keeping the surface smooth.

I need to check the end caps -- the tail cap is small and rounds off fine, but the nose dome at the front might extend further than the cowl recess can accommodate, potentially poking through the cowl's front lip.

Tracing out the polygon confirms it's a solid cowl shape with a recessed face, spanning from y 0 to 0.7 with the ring cut at 0.55. I'll give the fuselage a flat nose cap at z=1.6 while the cowl starts at z=1.4, setting up the caps definition.

For the cowl paint function, I'm defining recess areas as dark, the rim as yellow, and the rest with teal countershading based on height along the axis. I'm also checking the lathe options for orientation and segment count before moving to the vertical fin and rudder paint logic, where I want alternating teal/cream/red horizontal stripes using modulo arithmetic on the outline coordinates, being careful to handle negative values correctly.

Now I'm assigning colors to the elevator, stabilizer, wing, and ailerons—teal and red accents against cream bodies—while keeping flat color count low since paints and textures don't count toward the palette limit. Writing hull paint logic...

Still working out the stripe placement...

I want to add subtle mottled weathering to the base red color using nested paint functions, then move on to defining the wing paint with a cream-to-tan countershade gradient for the top surface.

Now I'm working out the tip region logic, using red coloring near the wingtip and leading-edge piping based on surface normal angles to mark the rounded nose area, plus thin tan rib lines spaced at regular intervals along the wing.

For the wing itself, I'm defining a swept path from one tip to the other with a tapered cross-section radius, keeping the span symmetric and adding rounded dome caps at each end to close off the tips.

I'm also considering roundel decals on the wing surfaces — placing them on the top and underside of the top wing for visibility from multiple angles, while deciding the bottom wing may only need one.

Now I'm adding nav lights: small glowing spheres at the wingtips, red on the left and green on the right, positioned at the leading edge extremity of the top wing dome.

For the ailerons, I'm extruding a thin profile shape and positioning it slightly below the wing centerline, skipping the control horn and pushrod details for simplicity.

Moving to landing gear, I'm detailing the shock absorber cylinders in gold, strut borders in red, and sweeping an elliptical cross-section along the axle for a cream/red fairing typical of Stearman-style gear.

Now I'm working out the tail wheel assembly, including a spring strut, a torus tire with its hub joint oriented along the X axis, and simplifying the fork into a single hub cylinder rather than separate rods. I'm also adding tail bracing wires as thin rods connecting the fin top to the stabilizer tips and struts beneath the stabilizer to the fuselage underside.

Then I move on to the pilot figure: a torso capsule sitting in the cockpit opening, shoulder-to-hand arm capsules angled forward to grip a control stick, with small spheres for hands and a thin rod representing the stick itself positioned between the pilot's hands.

Still writing pilot details...

Checking the mustache curve points against the head sphere's surface equation to make sure they sit just outside it rather than clipping through — the geometry is slightly off at the outer curl point, so I need to pull it back in.

Still working out mustache geometry...

Now I'm plotting the scarf as a flowing path trailing from the neck backward, positioning points down and back to give it a draped, wind-blown feel.

Good, the scarf stays clear of the fin, with a length around 1.1 units. I'm figuring out the color scheme—yellow with red stripe tips using banded coloring—and now working out the box section radius for the tube geometry.

Now I'm placing the ribbon with a flat horizontal orientation and a slight twist for flutter, then positioning the bear passenger: head, ears, muzzle, nose, and eyes all placed forward-facing above the wing so they stay clear of the surfaces.

I'm adding the bear's hidden body as a brown capsule rising from the cockpit, with small paw spheres resting on the front coaming, and a teal torus around the neck as a scarf knot instead of a bow tie. I'm also checking the windscreen placement against the bear's muzzle position to make sure nothing clips, confirming the bear sits toward the front of the cockpit.

I'm now working out seating: bear in front, pilot in the rear seat. I'm checking that the cabane strut feet near the rear cockpit don't collide with the coaming ring geometry, verifying the x and z positions of the struts against the ring's radius so nothing visually overlaps.

I shift the strut foot x-position slightly outward to .36 to clear the fuselage surface, then recompute the fuselage's half-width and half-height at each strut's z-station using the ellipse cross-section, checking that each foot sits just under the top surface for the front and rear strut pairs.

For the top attachment points, I'm placing cabane struts at (±0.62, 2.5) under the wing, verifying the wing's elliptical thickness profile keeps the underside above the attachment height at both the forward and aft positions. I settle on a circular rod of radius .035 for the cabane struts, colored like wood or red.

Now I'm checking the interplane struts: using a streamlined elliptical cross-section (ry=0.07 vertical, rx=0.018 horizontal) with rounded dome caps, running from y=1.2 to y=2.5, and confirming the dome ends stay tucked just inside the wing surfaces rather than poking through.

I'll skip strut fittings, collar rings, and wire attach plates as unnecessary detail, and skip the pushrod too.

For the propeller, I'm extruding a paddle-shaped blade outline at the hub position with rounded smoothing, orienting its thickness along the z-axis, and planning to paint tip and band stripes using the s-coordinate along the blade's length.

I'm checking the tip height clears the tail, mirroring the second blade downward with the same outline, and tapering the thickness from root to tip. Then I'm working out the hub cylinder and spinner lathe geometry, positioning the cowl recess, engine plate, and cylinder ring at the right z-depths so the hub, spinner base, and blades all line up correctly along the nose axis.

Finishing the spinner outline with finer resolution points for a smooth profile. Checking total fuselage length against real biplane proportions (~6.5m), which works out fine, and verifying the spinner base sits correctly within the cowl recess near the front lip.

I'm now placing the engine cylinders around the cowl radius, checking they stay hidden behind the lip while visible through the recess gap, then adding bolt/stud rings around the cowl seams and lip face as surface detail. Next I'm sketching the exhaust pipe sweep curves running from the lower cowl sides using a series of 3D points for a curved pipe path.

I'm skipping fuselage foot steps, and planning simple decal touches: a "7" number decal on the fin, a smiling sun-face texture, and a small set of pennant flag SVG textures with triangular colored shapes for bunting decoration.

For the pennant cards themselves, I'm reasoning through orientation: with lean 180 the card hangs downward with its apex pointing down, which matches a drooping pennant hanging from a line. I'm setting up the card frames, sizing, point count, and flow/sink parameters so the pennants drape naturally along the body.

For the connecting string, I'm sweeping a catmull-rom curve through three points (start, sagging midpoint, end) with a thin round-capped tube, dark brownish color, and then sampling positions along that curve to place each pennant frame.

Working through the start position though -- I need to check it clears the aileron flap geometry sticking out behind the trailing edge, so the string doesn't visually clip through the wing surface as x and z change along its path.

Checking the numbers, they'd nearly touch around x=3.05 where the aileron bottom and string path converge, but the margin stays just barely positive, so I'll leave it as is.

Now I'm setting the bunting string anchor point at the wing tip rear, and computing its length against the fin-top attachment point to make sure twelve evenly spaced pennants fit cleanly. I'm skipping extras like a hanging bell, and moving on to defining decal textures starting with a name label SVG.

I'm designing more decals -- a concentric roundel, a smiling sun face, a sunburst wheel, and a bold "7" for the fin -- then writing the placement logic that locates fuselage decal hit points by projecting onto the curved skin surface at a given azimuth and elevation.

For the name decal, I'm reasoning through orientation: the decal's direction follows the surface normal, up stays world-up, and I'm confirming no mirroring is needed since the text should read naturally unmirrored, unlike eye decals which mirror for the opposite side. I'm checking that the fuselage curvature at the chosen station gives a sensible height for centering the text.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the name text to clear the yellow stripe band, settling on a center around y=1.42 and narrowing the width to 1.3 so it fits within the tapering fuselage profile near the nose region.

I'm skipping the fuselage roundel idea and instead placing roundel decals on the top wing, casting a ray down from above the wing surface to find the hit point and applying an upward-facing decal with a forward-oriented "up" vector to avoid degenerate alignment with the surface normal. I'm also working out a similar approach for the underside roundel and for fin number decals, casting a ray inward from the side to locate the fin surface and center the artwork there.

For the cowl sun decals I'm computing hit points by sweeping around the cowl's circumference at ±90° azimuth to place them on the left and right sides, sizing them appropriately for the cowl radius, and making sure to handle the possibility that a ray cast returns no hit.

For the rivet rows, I'm casting rays along each fuselage side to find surface points, then building tiny sphere geometries offset slightly along the surface normal at each hit location, merging them all into a single part with the body's bone color rather than adding rivets individually.

I'm defining a helper that generates circular rings of points for additional fuselage details like windscreen frames and headrests, then moving on to the tail wheel and strut wiring, using a simple rod function with a square cross-section (4 sides) and flat caps for the wire connections hidden inside the wings.

Checking the type signatures for the rod, sweep, loft, extrude, and lathe builder functions to confirm how points, colors, and options are expected, and considering how outline arrays with mixed number/string tuples get inferred by TypeScript when left unannotated.

I'm also planning which imports will actually be needed—THREE, the builder constructor, randomness, catmull curves, paint/color utilities, texture functions—so I avoid unused import errors since I can't run a type checker to verify.

Defining the color palette...

Writing hull paint logic...

Settling on seam positions at roughly z=[1.15, -0.15, -1.0, -1.85] to cross the cockpit areas. Now I'm starting to define the fuselage shape as a loft through several cross-section stations along the body.

Checking that the fuselage's top profile clears the cockpit heights at each z-position, and confirming the caps option can take separate start/end styles with a rounded tail cap.

Now I'm working out the paint logic for the engine cowl lathe shape, distinguishing the recessed face from the lip and inner wall based on the normal direction and height along the profile, so I can assign colors like yellow for the lip and plum for the recess.

Working out the recess/lip radius logic with combined distance and color thresholds, then moving on to defining the lathe outline points for the cowl shape.

Checking that the cowl's bulbous radius creates a whimsical oversized nose relative to the fuselage, and considering whether the back flange needs a small collar ring to smooth the joint where cowl meets fuselage.

I'm now working out the windscreen geometry — a tilted glass panel with a frame of yellow rods, needing to compute the rotated local offsets to position the frame bars correctly around the angled glass.

For the cockpit, I'm sketching a helper that builds a disc for the seat base and a torus for the rim, oriented with a surface-normal direction to match the body's curve.

I need to figure out the right y-position so the disc sits flush with the fuselage top near z=-0.65, accounting for the curved surface dipping below the disc's flat edges at that radius.

For the pilot, I'm checking the torso capsule height against the head position to avoid overlap — adjusting torso top to y=1.93 so there's a small neck gap before the head center at 2.2.

Recalculating the head geometry: center at (0, 2.26, -0.68) with radius .17, clearing the wing underside. I'm placing the mustache points relative to this new head center and front face at z=-0.51, nudging the coordinates slightly to keep them seated correctly on the face.

Now I'm positioning goggles over the eyes as two lens cylinders along the z-axis, computing their forward offset so the lens surfaces sit flush against the curved forehead.

Making the googly eyes with cream-white lens color, plum pupils, and a white highlight. Now adding a strap torus around the head at the vertical axis, sized to wrap around the sphere's radius.

For the helmet, I'm using a partial sphere cut to cover the top and back of the head without blocking the goggles -- checking that the cap angle stops just above eye level so the face stays visible.

Working out the phi angle math so the helmet geometry leaves an open window at the front for the face, leaving most of the sphere covered except that front arc.

I'll settle on a thetaLength of about 72° for the helmet cap, bringing it down to roughly dy=.055, and position the goggles/eyes near the equator level so lens centers sit around y=2.255.

Now I'm working out positions for the lenses, cheeks, moustache, and nose using the face sphere's surface geometry -- computing dz values from dx offsets to place each feature so it sits flush or protrudes slightly from the face, with the nose using color "#f1a98a" and the mouth staying small since it'll be mostly hidden by the moustache.

Placing blush spheres embedded in the cheeks, adding leather earmuff flaps on the helmet sides, and topping it off with a small yellow pompom, keeping everything oriented away from the wing area before moving on to the pilot jacket.

Adding the shearling collar torus around the neck, positioning the trailing scarf path, and sketching arm capsules from shoulder to glove with brown leather gloves at the ends.

Now I'm placing a steel joystick between the hands with a red knob at the top, adjusting hand positions around it, and checking that the windscreen glass at the rear cockpit doesn't clip through the arms or stick.

I'm also figuring out the front cockpit coaming and windscreen positions, then starting to build the bear character itself — positioning the torso capsule, head sphere, and ears relative to the cockpit so the head clears the rim properly.

Now I'm placing the finer facial details on the bear: the inner ears, muzzle, nose, and eyes, working out the geometry so each feature sits correctly on the curved head sphere without poking through the surface.

I'm adding a teal scarf torus around the neck, considering a bow-tie but skipping it for simplicity, and placing brown paw spheres resting on the cockpit coaming. I'm grouping all these bear parts under a single head joint so they move together as one rigid piece.

Now I'm setting up the wheel joints mirrored left and right on the body, with tire torus geometry, a disc cylinder for the hub, and a sunburst decal plane oriented along the wheel's axis.

I'm adding a small steel bolt dome for the hubcap and sketching an axle fairing swept between the two wheel positions with tapered radii.

For the airfoil shape, I'm orienting the sweep so the chord runs along z with radius .13 and thickness along y at .04, colored red with flat body and flat caps. Now I'm starting to lay out the landing gear struts, placing rod geometry at offset positions for the front gear.

Deciding on colors, I land on teal for the struts and wheel hubs instead of matching the body color, since red would blend too much. I'm also adding a small thicker yellow sleeve mid-strut to represent the shock absorber, building a helper function that draws the main thin rod plus an offset sleeve segment using the lerp utility.

Now I'm defining the rear wheel strut geometry connecting to the axle point, then moving to the exhaust pipes -- sweeping a tapered steel tube along a curved path from the cowl down to the tip, with the open end tucked inside the cowl and the tip darkened with a burnt color band near the end.

I'm checking that the pipe placement stays within the cowl's radius at that cross-section so it reads as emerging from inside the body. Now I'm setting up joints for the rudder hinge and defining paint colors for the fin and stabilizer using the red coat gradient, then starting to sketch the outline points for the fin shape.

Working out fin outline coordinates...

The rudder sits at z=-2.9 with the hinge line straight at x=0, trailing edge at z=-3.48, giving an overall length of 5.9 from -3.48 to 2.44. Now I'm checking clearance between the elevator's trailing edge near z=-3.05 and the rudder's bottom relative to the elevator's height and thickness.

Now I'm shaping the horizontal stabilizer's outline, defining its swept contour from the root to a span of 1.45 with smoothing and bevel, oriented so its thickness runs along the vertical axis and colored in red. I'm checking that the fuselage width tapers correctly near the stabilizer's location so it fits flush against the hidden center section, then starting to define the paired elevator surfaces attached outboard of it.

Writing elevator outline coordinates...
